title: Fatimah and Ali
hook: the Prophet's daughter Fatimah marries Ali, and the bride price is a coat of armor (Abu Dawud)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Badr, the day itself: two young men in the row, and a verse that called the Muslims small. Your line was: few against many. Did you thank someone you hadn't expected much from? Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

A young man wants to marry, and he has almost nothing. That's Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin. The woman is Fatimah, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. In Medina, Ali asks for her hand, and the Prophet asks him: what will you give her? Ali says he has nothing. And the Prophet, who knows him well, asks a very practical question: where is your armor? Not a poem. Not a promise. Today: mahr.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN WITH ALMOST NOTHING.` → `WHAT WILL YOU GIVE HER?` → `WHERE IS YOUR ARMOR?`

segments.voice: The report is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, from Ibn Abbas. Ali says he has nothing to give, and the Prophet reminds him of his coat of armor, and that armor becomes the mahr, the bride's gift. In Islamic law the mahr belongs to the bride, not to her father. So the wedding of the Prophet's own daughter starts with a coat of mail. Another report, in the Sunan of an-Nasa'i, lists what the Prophet gave Fatimah for the new home: a cloth, a water skin, and a leather pillow stuffed with a fragrant grass. That's the whole list. A small house, a few things, and two people. Set beside it the advice the Prophet gave Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, the man from the market. In Sahih al-Bukhari, when Abd al-Rahman married, the Prophet told him to hold a wedding meal, even if only with one sheep. The meal mattered. The size didn't. And the marriage itself was ordinary in the best sense. Bukhari tells of a day the Prophet came to Fatimah's house and Ali wasn't there. She said there had been something between them, and he had gone out angry. The Prophet found him asleep in the mosque, his cloak slipped off and his side covered in dust. He began brushing the dust off him, saying: get up, Abu Turab. Father of dust. Ali, the report says, loved that name more than any other. A small quarrel, a father-in-law who came with a joke instead of a lecture. In Bukhari too, the Prophet says: Fatimah is a part of me. Sunni and Shi'a tradition both honor Fatimah and Ali, and this is where their household began: with very little, and with love.
screen: `THE MAHR WAS A COAT OF ARMOR.` · `A CLOTH, A WATER SKIN, A PILLOW.` · `A MEAL, EVEN WITH ONE SHEEP.` · `GET UP, ABU TURAB.` · then, large: `A SIMPLE WEDDING.`

segments.voice: The practice: keep a celebration simple. Sit, and settle your breath. Think of something coming up that you're meant to mark: a birthday, an anniversary, a graduation, a small win at work. Notice what you've been planning, and what it costs, in money and in worry. Now ask what the armor is: the one thing that actually matters in it. A meal together. A word said out loud. The right people in the room. Let the rest fall away for a moment. If you pray, you can ask Allah for blessing on the people you'll celebrate with. If you don't, just hold their faces in mind. The bell holds the time.
Mahr, the bride's gift. Fatimah and Ali married with a coat of armor for hers, and a home of very few things. Today's word.
Your line: a simple wedding. Today, cut one thing from a plan that's grown too big, and keep the meal, the word, or the people. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Muslim weddings vary widely by culture, but the mahr given to the bride and a walimah, a wedding meal, are part of the practice, and some couples keep both deliberately modest, remembering Fatimah and Ali.

options: wake him and tell him to go home and apologize.
brush the dust off him and call him father of dust.
leave him there and go back to your daughter.
fork.reveal: in Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ brushed the dust off Ali and said: get up, Abu Turab. Ali loved that name.

original.note: Arabic: the name of the Prophet's daughter, wife of Ali and mother of Hasan and Husayn.

trapdoor: what you thought: a famous couple.
what it means: a marriage begun with almost nothing, and a household Muslims honor.
what a scholar hears: the armor as mahr in Abu Dawud, the short list in an-Nasa'i, and Abu Turab in Bukhari.
recall: a narrow pass, away from crowds

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 2125 (Ibn Abbas: Ali has nothing to give; 'where is your armor?')
Sunan an-Nasa'i 3384 (what the Prophet prepared for Fatimah: a cloth, a water skin, a pillow stuffed with idhkhir)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5167 (hold a wedding meal, even with one sheep)
Sahih al-Bukhari 441 (Ali asleep in the mosque; 'get up, Abu Turab')
Sahih al-Bukhari 3714 (Fatimah is a part of me)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm Abu Dawud 2125 (armor as mahr), an-Nasa'i 3384 (the furnishings) and Bukhari 441, 3714, 5167.
'No great feast is recorded' is a soft claim about absence; a Keeper may know a report of the walimah (some sirah accounts describe one) and prefer to reword.
'Ali loved that name more than any other' paraphrases Sahl ibn Sa'd's remark in Bukhari 441 / 3703; confirm the wording.
'Muslims, Sunni and Shi'a alike, hold Fatimah and Ali in deep honor' is a general statement; confirm the phrasing is fair to both.
The practice describes asking for blessing in general terms, not a new prayer.

Editor: an-Nasa'i 3384 has the Prophet preparing these things for Fatimah, so 'what Fatimah brought' became 'what the Prophet gave Fatimah' (teach, match, source); cut the unsourced 'no great feast is recorded, no long procession' and the date claim 'around the same time'; 'Muslims, Sunni and Shi'a alike' softened to 'Sunni and Shi'a tradition both honor'.
